title: Find the largest element in an array (keep a variable `max`, update it when you find something bigger).
shortTitle: Find the largest element in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the largest element in an array is a linear scan algorithm. You initialise a `max` variable with the first element, then iterate through the remaining elements, replacing `max` whenever you find a value greater than the current `max`. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you touch each element exactly once and keep only a single tracking variable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants to know the single biggest deposit he made all year at National Bank of India. He takes his passbook, points at the first deposit and says "this is the biggest so far." Then he reads each later deposit one by one. Every time he sees a deposit bigger than the one he is pointing at, he moves his finger to that new bigger one. When he reaches the end, his finger is on the biggest deposit of the year.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start by assuming the first element is the biggest, then walk the array once and upgrade `max` whenever something larger appears.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the largest element in an array is a linear scan algorithm. You initialise a `max` variable with the first element, then iterate through the remaining elements, replacing `max` whenever you find a value greater than the current `max`. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you touch each element exactly once and keep only a single tracking variable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants to know the single biggest deposit he made all year at National Bank of India. He takes his passbook, points at the first deposit and says "this is the biggest so far." Then he reads each later deposit one by one. Every time he sees a deposit bigger than the one he is pointing at, he moves his finger to that new bigger one. When he reaches the end, his finger is on the biggest deposit of the year.

**One line to remember:** Start by assuming the first element is the biggest, then walk the array once and upgrade `max` whenever something larger appears.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is to hold one variable that remembers the biggest value seen so far. You must initialise it with a real element from the array, not with zero, because in banking a balance or an amount could be any value and starting at zero would give the wrong answer if all values were different in scale. In our examples amounts are always positive, but using the first element as the seed is the safe, correct habit.

The loop starts from index 1 because index 0 is already stored in `max`. For each element, you compare it with `max` using a simple greater-than check. If the element is bigger, you assign it to `max`. For example, if you are scanning monthly closing balances `balances[i].compareTo(max) > 0` tells you the current balance beats the record, so you update: `max = balances[i]`.

Because money must never use `float` or `double`, we use `BigDecimal` for amounts. `BigDecimal` does not support the `>` operator, so you compare with `compareTo`, where a result greater than zero means the left value is larger. A senior-level nuance is handling the empty array: if there are no elements there is no largest value, so you should throw an `IllegalArgumentException` rather than return a misleading zero.

The time complexity is O(n) — one pass. The space complexity is O(1) — just the `max` holder. You cannot do better than O(n) because you must look at every element at least once; if you skipped any element, that skipped element could have been the largest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to show Rajesh his "highest single transaction this month" on his statement page. His account SAV2001 has a list of transaction amounts for the month, and the system must find the single biggest one. This is exactly how the find-largest algorithm works — we keep a running record holder and upgrade it as we scan the list.

Problem 2 — If the month has no transactions at all, the list is empty, and there is simply no "largest transaction." A beginner program would return zero and mislead the customer into thinking a zero-rupee transaction happened. This is exactly why we guard the empty case and throw a clear exception instead of lying with a fake value.

The code will have an `Account` class holding `accountId`, `holderName`, and the list of transaction amounts. A `TransactionAnalyzer` class will have a `findLargestTransaction` method that performs the scan. The demo `main` loads Rajesh's amounts, calls the analyzer, and logs the largest amount found.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh's amounts list is `[12000.00, 450000.00, 8000.00, 275000.50]`.

Step 1 — The analyzer checks the list is not empty. It has four elements, so we proceed.

Step 2 — `max` is seeded with the first element, `12000.00`. This is our current record holder.

Step 3 — We compare the second element `450000.00` with `max`. Since `450000.00 > 12000.00`, we upgrade `max` to `450000.00`.

Step 4 — We compare the third element `8000.00` with `max`. Since `8000.00` is not greater than `450000.00`, `max` stays `450000.00`.

Step 5 — We compare the fourth element `275000.50` with `max`. Since `275000.50` is not greater than `450000.00`, `max` stays `450000.00`.

Step 6 — The loop ends. The analyzer returns `450000.00`, which the demo logs.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Largest transaction for Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) = Rs.450000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: amounts = [12000.00, 450000.00, 8000.00, 275000.50]
    │
    ▼
  TransactionAnalyzer.findLargestTransaction()
    │ empty check (4 elements)
    │ max = 12000.00            (seed with first)
    │ i=1: 450000.00 > 12000.00 ───→ max = 450000.00
    │ i=2:   8000.00 > 450000.00? no → keep
    │ i=3: 275000.50 > 450000.00? no → keep
    ▼
  return 450000.00
    │
    ▼
  Log: "Largest transaction for Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) = Rs.450000.00"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the largest element in an array is a classic linear scan problem that I solve in a single pass with constant extra space. I seed a maximum variable with the first element of the array, and then I walk through the rest of the array, comparing each element with my current maximum and upgrading the maximum whenever I find something bigger. By the time I reach the end, the maximum variable holds the largest value. The time complexity is linear because I touch each element once, and the space complexity is constant because I keep only one tracking variable.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used exactly this pattern to show a customer their highest single transaction for the month on their statement page. Rajesh's account has a list of transaction amounts, and I scan that list to find the biggest one. Because this is money, I store every amount as a BigDecimal and compare using the compareTo method, where a positive result means the left value is larger, since BigDecimal does not support the plain greater-than operator.

One nuance I always mention is the empty case. If the account has no transactions for the month, there is no largest value to return, so instead of returning a misleading zero I throw an IllegalArgumentException with a clear message. That way the calling code knows there was genuinely no data rather than believing a zero-rupee transaction occurred. This small guard is the difference between toy code and production code in a financial system.
